usage: Used when you want to gently correct a slight misunderstanding, state an alternative fact, or pause to structure your next sentence.
common_mistakes: Using 'actually' to mean 'currently' (now) due to native language interference.
Omitting the comma pause after 'actually' when speaking, which makes it sound rushed.
example_sentences: Well, actually, I prefer studying in the evening rather than early in the morning.
Well, actually, that is not quite what I meant to say.
Well, actually, I have never been to the UK, but I would love to go in the future.
Well, actually, the speaking test was much more relaxed than I expected.
Well, actually, we have already met once at a conference last year.
native_notes: Be careful with your intonation. If said too sharply, 'well, actually' can sound like you are correcting the other person in an arrogant way. Keep your tone soft and friendly.

usage: Used to return to your main point after you have been interrupted, gone off-topic, or used filler pauses.
common_mistakes: Saying 'How I was saying' (incorrectly translating the Uzbek 'qanday' or mixing up 'as' and 'how').
Saying 'As I said' when referring to a continuous explanation you were right in the middle of.
alternatives: Anyway, going back to my point...
To get back to what I was saying...
example_sentences: As I was saying, the main benefit of public transport is that it reduces traffic.
Anyway, as I was saying before the phone rang, we need to hire a new designer.
As I was saying, I really think we should focus on the local market first.
So, as I was saying, it is not as simple as it looks at first glance.
As I was saying earlier, I have always wanted to learn to play the violin.
collocations: as I was saying last night
native_notes: Use 'As I was saying' when returning to a thought that was active just seconds or minutes ago. Use 'As I mentioned earlier' if you are referring to something you said much earlier in the presentation or exam.
russian: Как я уже сказал... / Что касается меня...

usage: Used to explain or correct something you have just said, or to pause and think about how to rephrase your thought.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I mean that...' when used as a simple conversational filler.
Using it to translate direct literal meaning instead of as a transitional phrase.
alternatives: What I'm trying to say is
example_sentences: I think we should leave early, I mean, if we want to catch the first bus.
He's really nice—I mean, he always helps me with my homework.
I don't hate winter; I mean, I just prefer hot summer weather.
We could meet at three, or, I mean, four o'clock might be better for you.
It's quite a small flat—I mean, it only has one bedroom.
native_notes: 'I mean' is a highly effective way to correct a slip of the tongue in IELTS Speaking without losing points for coherence. You quickly say 'I mean' and give the correct word.
